summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the Appellate Division, the Court held that a municipality that assumes legal custody of a child by placing the child in foster care owes that child a common-law duty of care, so the plaintiff need not plead or prove a special duty to sue for negligent selection, retention, or supervision of the foster home.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling New York authority for a damages action by a child seriously harmed while in foster placement.
key_cases.quote: municipalities owe a duty of care to the children the municipalities place in foster homes because the municipalities have assumed custody of those children

key_cases.case_name: Doe v. New York City Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit reversed entry of judgment notwithstanding the verdict, holding that a foster-care placement agency may be liable under § 1983 where its supervisory personnel exhibited deliberate indifference to a known risk of abuse and that failure proximately caused the child's injury.
key_cases.relevance: It establishes that repeated warning signs ignored over years can support a jury verdict for a child seriously harmed in care.
key_cases.quote: we hold that entry of judgment n.o.v. for the defendant Bureau was unwarranted because the record contains sufficient evidence from which a jury could reasonably find deliberate indifference

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an action arising from an infant's death and the ensuing child-protective proceeding, the Second Circuit held that agency lawyers who initiate and prosecute child-protective petitions have absolute immunity, that caseworkers have only qualified rather than absolute immunity, and that qualified immunity nonetheless barred the § 1983 claims against the caseworkers here.
key_cases.relevance: The decision arises from a contested child-fatality investigation and defines the immunities that follow it.
key_cases.quote: The lawyer defendants are entitled to absolute immunity on plaintiffs § 1983 claims because they were performing functions analogous to those of a prosecutor

key_cases.holding: The Court held that no private right of action for money damages may be implied from title 4 or title 6 of article 6 of the Social Services Law for a child-welfare agency's failure to provide statutorily mandated services, because the Legislature enacted a comprehensive enforcement scheme centered on monitoring and loss of State reimbursement.
key_cases.relevance: Families of children harmed in agency care cannot base a damages claim on breach of the Social Services Law service mandates.
key_cases.quote: Recognition of such a private right of action under title 4 would not be consistent with the legislative scheme

key_cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of an abuse petition filed on behalf of a six-month-old who drowned, the Court held that a deceased child may be the subject of a Family Court Act article 10 abuse petition, because an adjudication that the parent abused or severely abused the child who died protects the surviving siblings, is admissible in a later proceeding to terminate parental rights, and preserves a judicial record of the circumstances of the death.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling New York authority requiring that a child fatality be adjudicated rather than closed as moot, so that the facts and circumstances surrounding the child's death become a matter of record and the surviving siblings receive the protection of Social Services Law § 384-b.
key_cases.quote: We thus reject the contention that a deceased child cannot be the subject of an abuse petition.
